source_text: Ἐὰν κάθῃ κρίνων, μὴ βλέπε ἀνώμαλα, μὴ τὸν πλού σιον ὑψηλὸν, τὸν δὲ πένητα ταπεινόν. Ἐὰν παραστῇ τῇ θύρᾳ σου ὁ τὴν χρείαν αὐτοῦ ἐπανορθωθῆναι ζη τῶν, μηδὲ οὕτως ἀνώμαλα ἴδῃς. Μὴ εἴπῃς· Οὗτος φίλος, οὗτος συγγενὴς, οὗτος εὐεργέτης· ἐκεῖνος ξένος, ἀλλότριος, ἄγνωστος. Ἀνώμαλα βλέπων, οὐκ ἐλεηθήσῃ· λεῖα βλέπε. Φύσις μία, ἄνθρωπος καὶ οὗτος κἀκεῖνος. Χρεία μία, ἔνδεια ἐν ἀμφοτέροις ἡ αὐτή. Δὸς τῷ ἀδελφῷ καὶ τῷ ξένῳ. Μήτε τὸν ἀδελφὸν ἀποστραφῇς, καὶ τὸν ξένον ἀδελφὸν οἰκεῖον ποίησαι. Λεῖα οὖν χρὴ βλέπειν. Μὴ πρόκρινε τὸν φίλον ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀλλοτρίου, τὴν χρείαν ἑαυτοῦ ἐπανορθούμενον. Βούλεταί σε παραμυθητικὸν εἶναι τῶν δεο μένων, οὐ προσωπολήπτην, οὐ τῷ συγγενεῖ διδόντα, τὸν δὲ ξένον ἀπωθούμενον. Πάντες συγγενεῖς, πάν τες ἀδελφοὶ, ἑνὸς πατρὸς ἔκγονοι πάντες. Ἐὰν τὸν πνευματικὸν ζητῇς πατέρα, ὁ οὐράνιος· ἐὰν τὰ γήινα ζητῇς, μήτηρ ἡ γῆ, καὶ ἀπὸ τοῦ αὐτοῦ πηλοῦ διηρτίσμεθα πάντες. Ὥστε ἀδελφὴ ἡ φύσις κατὰ σάρκα, ἀδελφὴ ἡ γένεσις ἡ κατὰ πνεῦμα. Τὸ αὐτό σοι αἷμα φορεῖ ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου ἀνθρώπου· τὴν αὐτήν σοι χάριν ἔλαβε παρὰ τοῦ Δεσπότου. Βλέπε οὖν λεῖα, ἵνα ἐλεηθῇς. Μὴ εἴπῃς· Οὗτος πλούσιος, καὶ τιμῆς ἄξιος· ἐκεῖνος πένης, καὶ φαυλίζω τὸν πένητα· μηδὲ ταῖς ὑπεροχαῖς ταύταις ἀνωμάλως διάνεμε τὰς τιμάς. Ἔστι γὰρ ὁ πλούσιος ψεύστης, ὁ πλούσιος ἅρπαξ, ὁ πλούσιος πόρνος, ὁ πένης δίκαιος. Μὴ τοίνυν τῇ ἔξωθεν ἐπιφανείᾳ πρόσεχε, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ κρυπτὸν εἰσερχόμενος, ἐκεῖ τὰς διαφορὰς διάνεμε. Τίμα τὸν τὰ τίμια κεκτημένον. Τί τιμιώτερον, ἀρετὴ ἢ πλοῦτος; Τί ἐκ τῶν ἔξωθεν δοκιμάζεις, τὰ κρύφια μὴ διερευνώμενος; Ὁρᾷς, ὅτι ὁ Βὴλ ἔξωθεν μὲν εἶχε χαλκὸν, ἔνδοθεν δὲ πηλὸν τῷ περιαστράπτοντι χαλκῷ ὑποκρυπτόμενον. Ἐὰν ἴδῃς τοὺς ἐν τῷ βίῳ περιφανεῖς, γίνωσκε, ὅτι χαλκὸς αὐτοῖς περιλάμπει, ἔνδοθεν δὲ πηλός εἰσι, τοῦ χαλκοῦ τὸ σαθρὸν ὑπερείδοντος. Πολλοὶ μὲν χρυσὸν ἔχουσιν ἔνδον, ὄστρακον δὲ ἔξωθεν περικείμενον. Οὗτος ὁ θησαυρὸς ὁ ἐν ὀστρακίνῳ σκεύει κεκαλυμμένος. Οὗτος σωφρονεῖ, κἀκεῖνος πορνεύει. Τίς πλουσιώτερος, ὁ τὴν σωφροσύνην ἔχων, ἢ ὁ τὰ χρήματα ἐξ ἀδικίας συνειλεγμένα; Τούτου τὸ μνημόσυνον ἀναφαίρετον· ἐκείνου ὁ πλοῦτος πρόσκαιρος. Τοῦτο κλέπτης οὐ διορύσσει· ἐκεῖνο σήμερον ἀνθεῖ, αὔριον δὲ ἀπομαραίνεται. Ὥστε βλέπε λεῖα, ὁμοτίμως κατὰ τὸ αὐτό· τὴν μέντοι διάκρισιν τῶν τιμίων μὴ ἀφανίσῃς, ἵνα ᾖς ἠλεημένος. «Καὶ ἀνδρὶ θυμώδει μὴ συναυλίζου.» Εἰπὲ δὲ ὅτι Ἔστι τις ἐν ἡμῖν φιλόδοξος, καὶ οὐ θυμικός. Φιλόδοξος εἶ; οὐ βλέπεις λεῖα. Θυμώδης εἶ; «Καὶ ἀνδρὶ θυμώδει μὴ συναυλίζου.» Εἶδες πῶς ἐν βραχυλογίᾳ ἡ διόρθωσις τῶν ἁμαρτημάτων δίδοται, ἐὰν μὴ ἄρα τὰ μὲν ὦτα κρουώμεθα διὰ τῆς φωνῆς, ἐπὶ δὲ τὴν καρδίαν τὴν ἔννοιαν τῶν λαλουμένων οὐ παραπέμπωμεν. Ἀλλ' ἐξέταζε μὲν, ποῦ τὸ ἐμὸν ἀνεγνώσθη; Τὰ περὶ τῶν θυμικῶν ἐπίγνωθι, ὁ θυμικός. Εἰπέ· Τοῦτο ἐμὸν τὸ πάθος· γνωρίζω τὸ ἀῤῥώστημά μου· λάβε τὴν θεραπείαν. Ἐὰν παρα στῇς τῷ ἰατρῷ, καὶ ἴδῃς τὴν πολυτέλειαν τῶν φαρμάκων ἐν ταῖς πολυπτύχοις ἀποκειμένην δέλτοις, περισκόπει τί οἰκεῖον ἀπόκειται τῷ σῷ πάθει.
thought_title: Look Without Favor on Rich and Poor
orientation: The preacher continues his exposition of impartiality, telling his hearers how to judge disputes and share goods without favoring kin, friends, or the rich over strangers and the poor.
pass_a_gloss: If you sit judging, do not look with partiality, do not look on the rich man as high and the poor man as low. If one who asks that his need be set right stands beside your door, not even thus look with partiality. Do not say: This one is friend, this one is kinsman, this one is benefactor; that one is stranger, alien, unknown. One who looks with partiality will not be shown mercy; look with impartiality. Nature is one, both this one and that one are human. Need is one, the same lack is in both. Give to the brother and to the stranger. Neither turn away from the brother, and make the stranger a brother of your own household. Therefore it is necessary to look with impartiality. Do not prefer the friend over the stranger, when he is getting his own need set right. He wishes you to be a comforter of those in need, not a respecter of persons, not one who gives to the kinsman and thrusts away the stranger. All are kinsmen, all are brothers, all are offspring of one father. If you seek the spiritual father, he is heavenly; if you seek earthly things, mother is earth, and we have all been fashioned from the same clay. So that nature according to flesh is sister, and birth according to spirit is sister. He wears the same blood as you from the first man; he received the same grace as you from the Master. Look therefore with impartiality, in order that you may be shown mercy. Do not say: This one is rich and worthy of honor; that one is poor, and I despise the poor man; nor with these superiorities distribute honors with partiality. For there is a rich man who is a liar, a rich man who is a robber, a rich man who is a fornicator, and a poor man who is just. Therefore do not attend to the outward appearance, but as you go in to the hidden place, distribute the differences there. Honor the one who has gained the things worthy of honor. What is more worthy of honor, virtue or wealth. Why do you judge from outward things, while you do not search through the hidden things. You see that Bel had bronze outside, but within clay hidden under the gleaming bronze. If you see those conspicuous in life, know that bronze shines around them, but within they are clay, since the bronze overlooks what is rotten. Many have gold within, but potsherd lying around outside. This is the treasure hidden in a vessel of potsherd. This one is chaste, and that one fornicates. Who is richer, the one who has chastity, or the one who has gathered money from injustice. The memorial of this one is not to be taken away; the wealth of that one is for a season. This a thief does not dig through; that blooms today, but withers tomorrow. So look with impartiality, with equal honor in the same way; yet do not efface the distinguishing of things worthy of honor, in order that you may be one who has been shown mercy. And do not lodge together with a man prone to anger. But say that there is someone among us who loves glory, and is not prone to anger. Are you one who loves glory. You do not look with impartiality. Are you one prone to anger. And do not lodge together with a man prone to anger. Did you see how in brief speech the correction of sins is given, unless we strike our ears with the voice, but do not send the meaning of the things said on to the heart. But examine, where was my passage read. Learn the things concerning those prone to anger, you who are prone to anger. Say: This is my passion; I know my sickness; take the cure. If you stand beside the physician, and you see the abundance of drugs laid up in tablets of many folds, look around for what is laid up that is fitting for your own passion.

pass_b_english: If you sit as a judge, do not look with partiality. Do not lift the rich man high and bring the poor man low. If a man stands at your door and asks for his need to be met, even then do not look with partiality. Do not say, "This man is a friend, this man is kin, this man is a benefactor, but that one is a stranger, an outsider, unknown." If you look with partiality, you will receive no mercy. Look with impartiality. Nature is one. This man and that man are both human. Need is one. The want in both is the same. Give to the brother and to the stranger. Do not turn away from your brother, and make the stranger your own brother.

So you must look with impartiality. Do not prefer your friend to the stranger who seeks to have his need met. He wants you to be a comfort to the needy, not someone who plays favorites, not one who gives to kin and drives the stranger away. All are kin. All are brothers. All are children of one Father. If you seek a spiritual father, he is in heaven. If you seek earthly things, earth is mother, and we were all fashioned from the same clay. So our nature in the flesh is sister, and our birth in the Spirit is sister. He bears the same blood as you from the first man. He received the same grace as you from the Master. So look with impartiality, so that you will be shown mercy.

Do not say, "This man is rich and worthy of honor, but that man is poor, and I despise the poor man." Do not hand out honors with partiality for outward rank. For the rich man may be a liar, the rich man a robber, the rich man sexually immoral, while the poor man is just. So do not fix your eyes on the outward show. Enter into what is hidden, and make your distinctions there. Honor the man who holds what is honorable. What is more honorable, virtue or wealth? Why do you judge by outward things and fail to search what is hidden? You see that Bel had bronze outside and clay inside, hidden under gleaming bronze. When you see men famous in this life, know that bronze shines around them, but inside they are clay, with the bronze propping up their rottenness.

Many carry gold within, with potsherd wrapped around the outside. This is the treasure hidden in a vessel of potsherd (2 Corinthians 4:7). One man lives chastely, and another lives impurely. Who is richer, the man who has chastity or the man whose money was gathered by injustice? The memory of the one cannot be taken away. The wealth of the other lasts for a season. No thief breaks through to steal the one. The other blooms today and withers tomorrow. So look with impartiality and honor each alike. Yet do not erase the distinction of honorable things, so that you may be shown mercy. Scripture says, "Do not lodge with a man prone to anger" (Proverbs 22:24).

But say, "There is someone among us who loves glory and is not quick-tempered." I answer you. If you love glory, you do not look with impartiality. If you are quick-tempered, Scripture says, "Do not lodge with a man prone to anger" (Proverbs 22:24). You see how correction for sins is given in few words, unless we only let the voice beat upon our ears and fail to send the meaning of what is said into the heart.

So examine yourself. Ask where your own passage was read. You who are quick-tempered, learn what is said about the quick-tempered. Say, "This is my passion. I know my sickness. Take the cure." When you stand beside the physician and see costly remedies stored in many-leaved books, look for what is stored there for your own affliction.
notes: Source text contains spaces inside words from line breaks, e.g. πλού σιον, ἐπανορθωθῆναι ζη τῶν, δεο μένων, πάν τες; read as continuous words and glossed accordingly

problems.quote: while the bronze outshines the decay
problems.why: The Greek says the bronze props up or underpins the rotten core. 'Outshines the decay' changes the image and loses the point that the bronze holds the rottenness up.
problems.fix: but inside they are clay, with the bronze propping up their rottenness.

problems.quote: You may say, "There is a man among us who loves glory but is not quick-tempered."
problems.source_quote: Εἰπὲ δὲ ὅτι Ἔστι τις ἐν ἡμῖν φιλόδοξος, καὶ οὐ θυμικός.
problems.why: εἰπέ is a command to name the case. English makes it a permitted objection.
problems.fix: But say, "There is someone among us who loves glory and is not quick-tempered."
problems.ruling: 'Εἰπὲ δὲ ὅτι' is an imperative ('Say that...'). 'You may say' turns it into a hypothetical objection, which changes the rhetorical force.

last_rejected.quote: Do not lift the rich man high and bring the poor man low.
last_rejected.source_quote: μὴ τὸν πλού σιον ὑψηλὸν, τὸν δὲ πένητα ταπεινόν
last_rejected.why: Governed by μὴ βλέπε: do not see the rich as high and the poor as low. English turns regard into lifting and humiliating.
last_rejected.fix: Do not look on the rich man as high and the poor man as low.
last_rejected.ruling: μὴ βλέπε ἀνώμαλα glosses 'do not look with partiality'; 'μὴ τὸν πλούσιον ὑψηλόν, τὸν δὲ πένητα ταπεινόν' means not seeing rich as high, poor as low. 'Lift high/bring low' is within range.
